newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS - Russia aluminium row not seen denting exports.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Russia aluminium row not seen denting exports.

text.p: Rows over foreign participation in Russia's giant aluminium industry should have no bearing this year on deliveries from the world's biggest exporter, a senior Russian aluminium official said on Wednesday.

"I think production and exports will remain stable through all of this," said Igor Prokopov, director general of the Kontsern Aluminiy producers' group, referring to recent comments by Russian officials that curbs might be in the works.
But the group urged government action on high energy and transportation costs, which Prokopov said were hurting the aluminium sector's long-term performance.
"The solution to these and other questions regarding the increasing competitiveness of Russian aluminium is only possible at a government level," a Kontsern Aluminiy statement said.
Russia supplies big Western aluminium users ranging from packagers to car makers.

Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov sparked the latest spat over foreign involvement in one of Russia's most lucrative industries by calling last month for protection of the sector from western firms operating major trade deals in Russia.
The call prompted a hostile and highly public response from the biggest single foreign player in the Russian aluminium business, the London-based Trans-World Group.
Its chairman, David Rueben, slammed Kulikov's comments earlier this week in full-page letters in the The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal.
World aluminium prices on the London Metal Exchange (LME) rose to a 14-month high of $1,701 a tonne on Tuesday, partly on concerns that such quarrels could disrupt exports to the West.
Kulikov's comments were short on detail, but they reflected growing concern within Russia that the industry depends too heavily on tolling deals with western commodity powerhouses.
Under tolling, western traders bring in raw materials, pay Russian plants to refine them, and then export the processed aluminium back to world markets.

Industry executives admit that tolling deals have allowed aluminium factories to boost production in recent years, while most other industries around them have contracted sharply after state support was abruptly withdrawn.
But now they say tolling robs Russia of the opportunity to earn more needed hard currency from refined aluminium exports.
Tolling accounts for nearly 70 percent of Russian primary aluminium output, which last year rose to 2.87 million tonnes from 2.79 million in 1995.
Of the 1996 total, 2.44 million tonnes were exported outside the Commonwealth of Independent States.
Prokopov forecast Russian primary aluminium exports stable in 1997 and said production would edge up two to three percent from 1996's level.
Moscow-based metal traders agreed that exports would remain stable, even if ownership quarrels raged on.

"Even if foreign ownership was curtailed, which is unlikely, Russia will still be exporting just about all of its output, because the government is desperate for cash," said a trader with a western trading firm.

Prokopov said low world aluminium prices hit Russian firms' profitability last year, as had rising costs of electricity and transportation. Russia's largest aluminium smelters are situated in southern Siberia, thousands of miles from western markets.
He also said the industry should continue to strive for greater integration by forming a smaller number of large firms grouping raw material suppliers with refining operations.

Prokopov said help may be on the way from higher aluminium prices, forecasting benchmark three-month futures on the LME to average $1,700-$1,800 a tonne in 1997, sharply higher than the 1996 average of $1,540.
He based the forecast on a positive outlook for world aluminium demand over the coming years.
